photographs.alt: A view from behind a cannon includes a pine-covered hillside and a flat, open valley beyond.
photographs.caption: View from the Howitzer Capture site
photographs.locationEvidence: Big Hole National Battlefield Site. When Colonel Gibbon moved his men on the night before battle, he gave instruction that the howitzer team follow with the gun at daybreak. This would allow for the surprise attach without the movement of the heavy gun betraying their presence. As the battle was underway in the river bottom, the howitzer team fired two shots from the hillside. A small group of Nez Perce quickly intercepted the gun crew and captured their gun, influencing the direction of the battle. This view still captures the strategic significance of the position.
photographs.changes: Resized NPS small version and encoded WebP; no visual alteration. Embedded EXIF/XMP preserved where present.

photographs.alt: Several pyramid-shaped lodges with structures of wooden poles mark the site of the historic encampment.
photographs.caption: Lodges at the Nez Perce Encampment Site
photographs.locationEvidence: Big Hole National Battlefield Site. These represent the lodges of Chief Joseph (right) and Ollocot (left) at the Nez Perce encampment. When the group made camp here in August of 1877, most had been on the move since early June, forced by the U.S. Army to leave their homelands to the west and resettle on the Nez Perce Reservation in Idaho. As the group evaded capture, they fought a series of battles and skirmishes in Idaho before crossing the Bitterroot Mountains.
